5.title: Children of the Day
5.overview:
After answering what happens to believers who die, Paul answers the next question, “When?”, by declining to give a date. The day of the Lord will come like a thief, suddenly, on a world saying “peace and security”. But believers are children of the day, so it will not catch them unprepared. They are to stay awake and sober, armed with faith, love and hope, because God has appointed them not to wrath but to salvation through Jesus, who died for them.

Then a run of instructions for church life: respect those who lead and work hard among you; warn the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with all; never repay evil; rejoice always, pray constantly, give thanks in everything; do not quench the Spirit, but test everything and keep what is good. The letter ends with a prayer that the God of peace will make them wholly holy, and a promise: “He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They know that the day of the Lord will come unexpectedly, like a thief in the night, and that sudden ruin will fall on those who feel secure. But believers are not in darkness, to be taken by surprise; they belong to the day. So they must stay awake and sober, wearing faith and love as a breastplate and the hope of salvation as a helmet. God has not appointed them to wrath but to salvation through Christ, who died for them so that, whether alive or dead at his coming, they will live with him. So they should encourage and build up one another.
verseByVerse.theology:
Not Destined for Wrath

God's purpose for his people was settled in advance, and settled on salvation rather than wrath (v.9) — not because of their performance but because the Lord Jesus ‘died for us’ (v.10), the only place in the letter where Paul states the substitution directly.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: ‘Peace and security’ was close to an imperial slogan, and Paul names it as the moment of collapse.

Now: Paul tells them what they are — children of the day — before he tells them to stay awake (vv.5–6). Getting that order backwards is what produces exhausted Christians.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the times and the seasons, brothers, you have no need to have anything written to you. For you yourselves are fully aware that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now concerning the times and the seasons, brothers, you have no need to have anything written to you. For you yourselves are fully aware that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.

Meaning first. 1 Thessalonians 5 turns from comfort about the dead to readiness for the living. No one knows when the day of the Lord will come: it will come like a thief, bringing sudden and inescapable ruin on people who feel secure (vv. 1–3). But believers are children of the day, so they stay awake and sober, armed with faith, love and hope, because God has appointed them not to wrath but to salvation through Christ, who died for them so that, alive or dead, they will live with him (vv. 4–11). Then comes life in the church: honour your leaders, give each struggling person the care he needs, never repay evil, rejoice, pray, give thanks, and test everything (vv. 12–22). The letter closes with a prayer and a promise: the faithful God will sanctify them completely for Christ’s coming, and his grace goes with them (vv. 23–28).

Now concerning the times and the seasons, brothers. Chapter 4 answered the question they had asked: what about our dead? Chapter 5 answers the next one: when? Paul’s answer is a polite refusal. Chronos is clock time, how long; kairos is the appointed moment, at what point. Paul declines both.

Echoing his Lord. He is echoing Jesus, who told the disciples that it was not for them to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority (Acts 1:7), the same pair of words. And they needed nothing more written: in a stay of a few weeks Paul had taught them not a schedule but a certainty and a posture.

The day has a face. The day of the LORD comes from the prophets: the day God settles accounts, darkness and not light for people who assumed it would be good news for them (Amos 5:18–20; Joel 2:31). Paul hands that name to Jesus without a word of explanation, and so the day now has a face. The Lord who is coming is the Jesus they already know, who came once, openly, to die for them (v. 10), and will come again to gather the people he died for. That is why Paul can leave the date unknown and the church unafraid. For the secure world the day is ruin; for those in Christ it is the arrival of their Saviour, because the darkness the prophets warned of has already fallen once, on him.

Like a thief. The image comes from Jesus himself (Matthew 24:43; 2 Peter 3:10; Revelation 16:15). A thief is not dangerous because he is malicious but because he does not send word. The image is about unannouncement, not menace, which is why calculating the date is not merely difficult but a contradiction of the teaching.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the day will be secret. It will be sudden, but visible to all.

Then why do so many people try to work out the date? Because uncertainty is uncomfortable, and a date feels like control. But every attempt has failed, and some have done real harm: believers who sold homes, quit jobs or lost faith when the date passed. Jesus said that even the angels do not know (Matthew 24:36). The right response to not knowing when is to be ready always. If someone tells you they have found the date, or that it must be within a certain number of years, you can kindly set it aside. The Lord has told us everything we need, and he has not told us that.

Should the signs in the news make me think the end is very near? The end may be near; it has been near, in the biblical sense, since the ascension (Romans 13:11–12; James 5:8). Wars, earthquakes and troubles are, Jesus said, the beginning of the birth pains, not the end itself (Matthew 24:6–8), and they have marked every age. Read the news as a reminder that this world is passing, not as a code to crack. Live each day as though he might come today, and plan your life as though he might not come for a hundred years. Both are faithful.

In a sentence. Now, brothers and sisters, about times and dates we do not need to write to you, for you know very well that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.

On a Tuesday. Do not try to calculate the date of Christ’s return. Be ready for it today. Ask what you would want to have finished, forgiven, said or given up if he came this week, and do that.

For worship. The Father has fixed the day by his own authority, and he has not told us, and that is good. Our future is not in a calendar but in a Person. The Lord who comes like a thief to the sleeping world comes as a bridegroom to his waiting bride. Blessed be the Lord of the day, whose timing is perfect and whose coming is sure.

verseByVerse.quote: While people are saying, "There is peace and security," then sudden destruction will come upon them as labor pains come upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While people are saying, “There is peace and security,” then sudden destruction will come upon them as labor pains come upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape.

While people are saying, There is peace and security. Those two words together, eirēnē kai asphaleia, were very close to a Roman slogan. The pax Romana was the empire’s proudest claim and its central promise: peace, and safety, guaranteed by the legions. Coins and inscriptions said so. Thessalonica, a free city that had backed the winning side in Rome’s civil wars and prospered for it, had every reason to believe the advertising. So had Jerusalem when its false prophets said peace, peace, when there was no peace (Jeremiah 6:14). Paul quotes the slogan at the very moment of collapse: a civilisation announcing its own permanence is the least prepared thing there is.

Another king, Jesus. The slogan had a rival in Thessalonica from the first weeks. The mob that dragged Jason before the city rulers charged the believers with acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus (Acts 17:7). The charge was truer than they knew. Rome offered peace won by the sword. Christ made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), and he himself is our peace (Ephesians 2:14). His peace was secured when he took on himself the ruin this verse describes, and it is the only peace and security that will still be standing on the day of the Lord.

Then sudden destruction will come upon them. The word is olethros, ruin: not annihilation, but eternal loss, the shutting out from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:9).

As labour pains come upon a pregnant woman. Labour is sudden in its onset: no one is told the hour. But it is not unexpected: the woman has known for months that it is coming, and it does not arrive out of nowhere. That is the exact combination Paul wants. The day is unpredictable in timing and entirely predictable in fact. Anyone claiming to be taken by surprise had the information all along.

And they will not escape. The negative is emphatic: they will by no means get clear. Once labour starts it cannot be called off; it has to be gone through.

A future the slogan never had. The image is not only severe. Labour ends in a birth, and the New Testament uses birth-pain language for the end of the age because the pains precede something being born, a new creation (Romans 8:22). Paul does not develop it here; he is writing about those who are caught out. But the picture he chose carries a future the slogan never had.

What it does not mean. It does not mean peace is bad. It means false security apart from God is deadly.

Is this destruction really eternal? Is hell real? Yes. The destruction of the day of the Lord is not a temporary trouble but final ruin, described elsewhere as eternal destruction away from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:9) and as conscious, unending punishment (Matthew 25:46; Revelation 14:11). It is the most sobering truth in Scripture, and Jesus spoke of it more than anyone. It is not taught to frighten Christians, who are not destined for wrath (v. 9), but to wake the sleeping while there is time, and to show us what Christ saved us from.

Where do I find false security in my own life? Wherever you feel safe without God: in savings, health, a career, a good reputation, a country’s stability, or even a past religious experience you no longer live by. None of these is wrong to have; all are wrong to rest on. Ask what you would still have if each were removed tomorrow. The only security that survives the day of the Lord is being in Christ.

In a sentence. While people are saying, Peace and safety, destruction will come on them suddenly, as labour pains on a pregnant woman, and they will not escape.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone around you who feels secure without God. Pray for them by name, and ask God for an opening to speak to them about the only safety that lasts. And examine your own securities: thank God for them, and rest on him alone.

For worship. Empires announce their permanence and fall; the kingdom of the Son cannot be shaken (Hebrews 12:28). The pains that will seize the secure world will end, for his people, in a birth: a new heaven and a new earth. And the first of that new creation has already been born. Christ passed through the anguish of the cross and came out of the tomb as the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18), the pledge that everything the pains are leading to will be his. Blessed be the King whose peace is no slogan, and whose people will see a morning no empire ever imagined.
verseByVerse.note: “Peace and security” may echo the boasts of the Roman order.

parallels.desc: Peace, peace, when there is no peace

verseByVerse.quote: But you are not in darkness, brothers, for that day to surprise you like a thief. For you are all children of light, children of the day. We are not of the night or of the darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you are not in darkness, brothers, for that day to surprise you like a thief. For you are all children of light, children of the day. We are not of the night or of the darkness.

But you are not in darkness, brothers. But you, and the whole paragraph turns from the people saying peace and security to the church. Paul does not say they will avoid the day, but that it will not surprise them. Darkness in Scripture means ignorance, sin and unbelief, and they have been brought out of it.

For that day to surprise you like a thief. The thief is a problem for the household that is asleep, not for a house with its lights on. The difference is not in the thief’s timing but in who is awake. Believers do not know the date, but they will not be caught unprepared.

For you are all children of light, children of the day. Then the identity, and it comes before any command. The Hebrew idiom son of means belonging to, characterised by: sons of light are people whose nature is light (Ephesians 5:8). That means God has given them a new heart. Where once they loved the dark and hid from God, they now love what is true and want their deeds to be seen as done in God (John 3:19–21). Paul is not telling them to become something; he is telling them what they are. And the little word all matters: not only the mature or the leaders, but every believer, including the fainthearted and the weak of verse 14.

Believe in the light. The phrase sons of light comes from the lips of Jesus. While you have the light, he told the crowds in Jerusalem, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light (John 12:36); and he had already said who the light was (John 8:12). So the light these believers belong to is not a moral climate. It is a Person, and they became his by believing in him. The day they belong to is his day, and they are its children because they are already joined to him. That is why Paul slips at once from you to we: he is one of them.

Identity before command. Paul’s ethics always follow this order, and getting it backwards produces exhausted Christians. He does not say: stay awake, and then you will be children of light. He says: you are children of light, therefore stay awake.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are already perfect. It means they belong to a different realm.

How did I become a child of light? By God’s act, not yours. God, who said let light shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). He delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son (Colossians 1:13). You did not climb into the light; the light came to you. That is why the word all can stand: every believer is there by the same grace.

I still do things that belong to the darkness. Am I really a child of light? If you trust Christ, yes. Children of light still sin, but they no longer belong to the night, and they cannot be at home there. The sign is not sinlessness but what you do with sin: you hate it, bring it into the light by confessing it, and turn from it (1 John 1:7–9). Live like what you are. When you stumble in the dark, remember whose child you are and walk back toward the light.

In a sentence. But you, brothers and sisters, are not in darkness so that this day should surprise you like a thief. You are all children of the light and children of the day. We do not belong to the night or to the darkness.

On a Tuesday. You are a child of the light. Live in the light today, with nothing to hide. Is there anything in your phone, your accounts, your private habits or your heart you would not want seen when the day dawns? Bring it into the light now, before God, and if needed before a trusted brother or sister.

For worship. God is light, and in him is no darkness at all. Yet the light of the world went into the dark for us. At noon on the day he died, darkness came over all the land, and he was forsaken in it, so that children of the night could be called children of the day. Now the night is far gone and the day is at hand, and we belong to it already, because we belong to him. Glory to the Son, who entered our night so that we could belong to his morning.

verseByVerse.quote: So then let us not sleep, as others do, but let us keep awake and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk, are drunk at night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then let us not sleep, as others do, but let us keep awake and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk, are drunk at night.

So then let us not sleep, as others do. The sleep here is not the sleep of 4:13–15, where it was a tender word for the Christian dead. Paul has changed its use deliberately within a page. Here it is spiritual carelessness: the drowsiness of a person who has stopped paying attention. And note let us: Paul does not consider himself immune.

But let us keep awake and be sober. Two positive commands answer it. Keep awake (grēgoreō): the word for the watchman, and for the disciples in Gethsemane, who failed at it. And be sober (nēphō): the opposite of intoxicated; clear-headed, self-controlled, in possession of your judgement, able to see what is actually there.

Watching for the master of the house. Keep awake is Jesus’ own word, and he gave it a picture. A man goes on a journey, gives each servant his work, and tells the doorkeeper to stay awake, because no one knows whether the master will come in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow or in the morning (Mark 13:33–37). Christian wakefulness is not nervous vigilance against an unknown danger. It is a servant listening for a footstep he loves: the Lord who went to prepare a place for his people and promised to come again and take them to himself (John 14:3).

The underrated virtue. Sobriety is the underrated Christian virtue. It is not solemnity: this letter commands rejoicing ten verses later. It is the capacity to assess things accurately, to know what is temporary and what is permanent, and not to be talked into a false estimate of either. Drunkenness is the standing biblical picture of misjudgement, of a man who thinks he is fine and is not.

For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk, are drunk at night. In the ancient city the night belonged to sleeping and carousing, and the day to work (Romans 13:12–13). The argument is one of fitness. Sleep and drunkenness belong to the dark, and these people do not belong to the night at all. So moral drowsiness in a Christian is out of place, like a man asleep in the street at noon. Paul is not threatening them into wakefulness; he is pointing out that they are dressed for the wrong hour.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should never sleep or relax. It means they should never be spiritually careless.

What does spiritual sleep look like in an ordinary Christian? It rarely looks like rebellion. It looks like drift: prayer becoming occasional, the Bible unopened for weeks, church attended without attention, sins no longer noticed, eternity no longer thought about, the heart filled with screens and schedules until God is crowded out. The sleeper does not feel asleep. That is why Paul says let us: we need one another to notice and to wake each other up.

Does be sober forbid alcohol? Scripture does not forbid alcohol itself; wine is a gift that gladdens the heart (Psalm 104:15), and Jesus made it. It does forbid drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18), and here it uses drunkenness as a picture of a dulled mind. Some Christians choose to abstain, for their own sake or for others, and that is a wise freedom. Whatever you drink, never let anything, alcohol, entertainment, busyness or anxiety, cloud your judgement about what matters most.

In a sentence. So then, let us not be like others, who are asleep, but let us be awake and sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk, get drunk at night.

On a Tuesday. Ask God to keep you spiritually awake and clear-headed today. Then take one practical step against drift: a fixed time for Scripture and prayer, a screen turned off, a friend asked to check on you. Wakefulness is kept by habits, not just resolutions.

For worship. In Gethsemane the disciples slept, and the Lord Jesus stayed awake for them, sweating in prayer while they dozed. He kept watch when we could not, and now he keeps watch over us. He neither slumbers nor sleeps, and by his Spirit he wakes his people up. Blessed be the watchful Saviour, who will find his children ready.

verseByVerse.quote: But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation.

But since we belong to the day, let us be sober. Now Paul says how a person actually stays awake. Sobriety is not achieved by trying harder to concentrate. It is achieved by getting dressed.

Having put on the breastplate of faith and love. The picture is a soldier on night watch, and Paul is drawing on Isaiah, where the LORD himself puts on righteousness as a breastplate and a helmet of salvation on his head (Isaiah 59:17). Paul will develop the same image at length in Ephesians 6:14–17.

The armour the Redeemer wore. In Isaiah the LORD arms himself because he looks and sees no one to intervene, so his own arm brings salvation; and the passage ends with the promise that a Redeemer will come to Zion (Isaiah 59:16–20), words Paul applies to Christ (Romans 11:26). The armour was first worn by the one who came to save, alone, where no one else could stand, and he now gives it to those he rescued. Believers are not sent out to win their own salvation; they are clothed in the gear of a victory already won, and the helmet is the hope of a salvation that comes, as the next verse says, through our Lord Jesus Christ.

The triad returns. The armour is made of faith, love and hope, the triad of the letter’s first paragraph (1:3). What Paul thanked God for in chapter 1 he now hands them as protection.

And for a helmet the hope of salvation. The placement matters. Faith and love cover the chest: trust in God and love for others keep you alive. Hope is the helmet: it keeps you thinking straight. A church losing its grip on the future does not merely become sad; it becomes unable to think clearly about the present, which is what had happened when their friends died. And the armour is entirely defensive. There is no sword here. Paul is equipping them to stay upright until the day comes.

What it does not mean. It does not mean hope is uncertain wishing. It is confident expectation.

What does it mean to put on faith, love and hope in practice? It means deliberately taking hold of them each day, as a soldier straps on armour before the watch. Put on faith by reminding yourself of God’s promises and trusting them in the decisions in front of you. Put on love by deciding, before you meet people, to seek their good. Put on hope by setting your mind on Christ’s return and your inheritance, especially when discouragement starts to talk. You do this through Scripture, prayer and the fellowship of the church, which is where the armour is kept.

Is the hope of salvation certain, or might I lose it? Certain, because it rests on God’s appointment, as the next verse says: God has not destined us for wrath but to obtain salvation. Biblical hope is not maybe; it is a sure thing not yet seen (Romans 8:24–25). It is called a helmet precisely because it holds when you are struck. If you are in Christ, your future salvation is as secure as his resurrection.

In a sentence. But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, putting on faith and love as a breastplate, and the hope of salvation as a helmet.

On a Tuesday. Put on your armour today: faith in God, love for others, hope of salvation. Before you leave the house, name one promise to trust, one person to love, and one reason to hope. And when an attack comes, discouragement, fear, temptation, notice which piece of armour it is aimed at, and hold it up.

For worship. The Lord who arms his people went into his own battle stripped. For our helmet he wore thorns; for our breastplate his side was opened by a spear. He took the blows unguarded so that faith, love and hope could cover us through the night. Now nothing aimed at the heart or the head of his people can finish them, because the one who stood exposed for them stands risen for ever. Glory to the Warrior who was stripped for us, and dresses his soldiers for the dawn.

parallels.desc: righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation

verseByVerse.quote: For God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him.

For God has not destined us for wrath. Here is the ground under everything, and it answers the fear that the wrath language has been raising since 1:10. The verb (tithēmi) means to appoint, to set in place beforehand: God’s purpose settled in advance. And it is settled not on wrath, God’s final judgement (1:10). Whatever the day of the Lord means for the world, it does not mean that for these people, and the reason is not their performance.

But to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ. God appointed them to salvation: this is election again (1:4; 2 Thessalonians 2:13). To obtain salvation is a word for acquisition, coming into possession. Salvation here is still ahead of them, something to be come into, as an heir comes into an estate. Paul can speak of salvation as past, present and future, and here it is the future he needs: they are not hoping to be spared; they are on their way to collect.

Who died for us. There is the mechanism, and it is the only place in this letter where Paul states the substitution directly. For us (hyper hēmōn) means on our behalf and in our place. Why are they not destined for wrath? Not because God overlooks things. Because someone else stood where they were standing, and bore the wrath himself. The basis of salvation is Christ’s substitutionary death.

So that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him. Then the clause that ties the two chapters together. Paul reaches back to 4:13–18: awake meaning alive, asleep meaning dead, at Christ’s return. The Thessalonians had been frightened that the dead would be at a disadvantage. Paul says the death of Jesus settled that too: alive or dead when he comes, the outcome is identical. No believer misses out.

Does this mean the church will be taken away before the tribulation? Pretribulational Christians argue so: the church is not destined for wrath, so it cannot go through the tribulation. But wrath here is God’s final judgement, from which Jesus delivers us (1:10; Romans 5:9), not the trouble Christians may suffer in this world, which Paul says they are destined for (3:3). Believers are kept from God’s wrath, not from every tribulation.

Where Christians differ: not destined for wrath. Some use this verse to argue that believers will be raptured before a future tribulation. Verdict: The wrath here is God’s final judgement on the ungodly, from which Christ’s death saves believers (1:10; Romans 5:9). It does not promise exemption from suffering or persecution before the end; the Thessalonians were already suffering (3:3). Believers will be delivered from God’s wrath, not from all tribulation (John 16:33; Acts 14:22).

The real comfort. And that is the real comfort of the passage. Not that they will be alive at the parousia: Paul does not know and does not promise it, and in fact every one of them died. The promise is that it will not matter. We might live with him is the same note that ended chapter 4: always with the Lord.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers can live carelessly. Those destined for salvation live as children of the day.

Why did Christ have to die for us? Could God not simply forgive? God’s forgiveness is free to us but not cheap. Sin is a real offence against a holy God, and a just judge cannot simply ignore it (Exodus 34:7; Romans 3:25–26). The wonder of the gospel is that God himself, in the person of his Son, took the penalty, so that he could be both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. Christ died for us: in our place, under our condemnation, so that the wrath we deserved is spent and gone. That is why God can say to believers, with perfect justice, you are not destined for wrath.

How do I know I am destined for salvation and not wrath? Not by peering into God’s decrees but by looking to Christ. Do you trust him who died for us? Then this verse is about you. Those whom God appointed to salvation, he calls to faith (Romans 8:30), and faith is the sign of the appointment. If you are afraid, do not look first at your feelings or your record; look at the cross, where the wrath fell on him, and rest there.

In a sentence. For God did not appoint us to suffer wrath but to receive salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ. He died for us so that, whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with him.

On a Tuesday. When fear of judgement or death rises today, answer it with this verse word for word: God has not destined me for wrath, but to obtain salvation through my Lord Jesus Christ, who died for me. Say it until you believe it again, and then go and live as an heir.

For worship. The Father appointed us to salvation before the world began. The Son died for us, in our place, and drank the cup of wrath to the dregs. And now, alive or dead, we shall live with him. There is no condemnation left, no wrath stored up, no case pending. Glory to the Lord Jesus, who went into death awake to all its horror, so that his people, awake or asleep, would never be anywhere but with him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore encourage one another and build one another up, just as you are doing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore encourage one another and build one another up, just as you are doing.

Therefore encourage one another and build one another up. It is the second time in two paragraphs that Paul has ended a passage about the last day with an instruction to talk to each other (4:18). Teaching about the end is not given to satisfy curiosity or to sort Christians into camps; it is given to be used on people who need it.

What they are to say. The first word of the verse, therefore, points back to the content. The encouragement Paul means is not general cheerfulness but the sentence he has just written: Christ died for us so that, awake or asleep, we will live with him. That is the material the building is raised from. One believer reminding another that the wrath has been borne and the future is fixed is laying Christ again as the foundation (1 Corinthians 3:11), and every course of bricks goes up on him. A church whose members talk to each other about Christ’s cross and coming is a building going up; one that only talks about itself is a site with no foundation.

Build one another up. The word is oikodomeō, constructing a building, behind our word edify: something raised course by course, to a plan. Encouragement is not generalised niceness; it is structural work on another person. And it is one another: not Paul, and not the leaders of verse 12, but ordinary members who know enough doctrine to have something to say and know each other well enough to know when to say it.

Just as you are doing. Once more the gracious ending (4:1, 10). Paul does not correct a fault they do not have. He names what is already true and asks for more of it, which is a harder discipline than criticism, and a good deal more effective.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only leaders encourage. All believers do.

How do I build someone up if I am not a teacher? With ordinary words, aimed well. Tell someone specifically where you see God’s grace in them. Share a verse that helped you this week. Remind a discouraged friend of a promise. Ask how you can pray, and then do it, and tell them you did. Thank someone for serving. Speak hope about Christ’s return to someone who is weary. Building up is usually a sentence at a time, given at the right moment, and anyone who loves Christ and his people can do it.

In a sentence. Therefore encourage one another and build each other up, just as in fact you are doing.

On a Tuesday. Encourage one fellow believer today with the hope of Christ’s return. Choose someone in particular, a tired parent, an elderly saint, a struggling young Christian, and add one course of bricks to what God is building in them.

For worship. The Lord Jesus said, I will build my church, and nothing has stopped him. He gathers living stones out of the rubble of sinners, and he uses our small words of encouragement as his tools. One day the building will be finished, and he will present it to his Father without a crack in it. Blessed be the Builder, who lets us lay bricks beside him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul asks them to respect and love those who labour among them, lead them and admonish them, and to live at peace. They should warn the idle, encourage the timid, help the weak and be patient with everyone; never repay evil for evil but always seek good. They are to rejoice always, pray continually and give thanks in every circumstance, which is God’s will in Christ. They must not quench the Spirit or despise prophecy, but test everything, holding on to what is good and avoiding every kind of evil.
verseByVerse.theology:
Discernment Instead of Either Extreme

Verses 19–22 refuse both easy positions: not contempt for what the Spirit gives, and not credulity, but testing — holding fast what is good and abstaining from what is bad. A church asked to be both open and awake has the harder, better task.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A congregation only months old already had people labouring, leading and admonishing, honoured ‘because of their work’ (v.13).

Now: Verse 14 asks every member, not only leaders, to read the person in front of them: the idle need admonishing, the fainthearted encouraging, the weak holding up. And verse 18 asks for thanks in all circumstances, not for them.

verseByVerse.quote: We ask you, brothers, to respect those who labor among you and are over you in the Lord and admonish you, and to esteem them very highly in love because of their work. Be at peace among yourselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We ask you, brothers, to respect those who labor among you and are over you in the Lord and admonish you, and to esteem them very highly in love because of their work. Be at peace among yourselves.

We ask you, brothers, to respect those who labour among you. Three descriptions of the same people, and they are not three offices but one job seen from three sides. They are church leaders, probably the elders, though the word is not used. They labour among you: kopiaō, the exhausting word from 1:3, work to the point of weariness. They are over you in the Lord: proistēmi, which means to stand in front of, and carries both leading and caring for. And they admonish you: noutheteō, to put in mind, the word for correction that is meant to change someone.

How young this was. This church was months old, and it already had recognised leaders, described not by title but by their work, the only credential on offer. The congregation owes them two things. The first is respect, literally to know them: to recognise them for what they are, which means noticing who is doing the work.

And to esteem them very highly in love because of their work. The phrase is emphatic; Paul stacks the intensifiers again (hyperekperissou, beyond all measure, the word of 3:10). But the ground is stated exactly: not because of their office, their gifts or their personality, but because of their work. And in love, not merely as duty. That cuts both ways: the honour is tied to something real rather than to status, and a congregation that grasps what the work costs, the broken nights, the conversation nobody wants to have, will find the esteem easier to give.

Over you in the Lord. Two words keep this from becoming an ordinary chain of command. Their leadership is in the Lord: exercised inside Christ’s rule and answerable to him. They are not lords over the flock (1 Peter 5:3). They serve the one Lord, who said that whoever would be first must be slave of all, and who came not to be served but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:44–45). So a church that honours its faithful leaders is honouring Christ’s gift, and a leader who domineers has forgotten whose flock it is.

Be at peace among yourselves. The clause reads like an aside, but it is deliberate. Attitudes to leadership are one of the commonest fault lines in a congregation, and having told them to esteem certain people very highly, Paul guards it: not so highly that you form parties around them. Peace among the members is the condition in which anyone can lead at all, and it honours Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean leaders are above correction. It means they deserve honour and love.

What if my church leaders get things wrong? They will, because they are sinners like you. Honour does not mean pretending they are perfect. Pray for them first. If something is a matter of preference, let it go graciously. If it is a real concern, go to them privately and humbly, as you would want to be approached (Matthew 18:15). If there is serious sin or false teaching, Scripture gives a careful process (1 Timothy 5:19–20). And abuse of any kind must never be covered up: it is to be brought into the light and, where it is a crime, reported, whoever the leader is. Respect for leaders never means silence about harm.

How do I actually show esteem to my pastor and elders? Pray for them by name, regularly. Tell them specifically when their ministry has helped you. Receive their teaching and admonition without resentment (Hebrews 13:17). Do not gossip about them or join in when others do. Support them practically, including generously providing for those who teach (1 Timothy 5:17–18; Galatians 6:6). Care for their families. Turn up and serve. A leader who knows he is loved can bear far more of the work.

In a sentence. Now we ask you, brothers and sisters, to acknowledge those who work hard among you, who care for you in the Lord and who admonish you. Hold them in the highest regard in love because of their work. Live in peace with each other.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for your church leaders by name. Then tell one of them this week, in a note or a sentence after church, one specific way their work has helped you. It costs you a minute, and it may carry them through a hard month.

For worship. The Lord Jesus is the Chief Shepherd, and he gives under-shepherds to his flock, labouring men who will give account for our souls. Every faithful pastor is his gift and a small picture of his care. He laboured for us to the point of death, and he leads us in love. Glory to the Shepherd and Overseer of our souls.

verseByVerse.quote: And we urge you, brothers, admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we urge you, brothers, admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with them all.

And we urge you, brothers. Now Paul turns from what the congregation owes its leaders to what its members owe each other, and three different people get three different treatments. All the brothers are addressed, not just leaders.

Admonish the idle. The word ataktoi is military: the soldier out of rank, disorderly. It is the same problem as 4:11: those who had stopped working, very likely because of excitement about the Lord’s return (2 Thessalonians 3:6–12). What they need is not sympathy. They need to be told.

Encourage the fainthearted. Oligopsychoi, literally small-souled: the person whose courage has run low, discouraged, anxious. In a church losing members to persecution and burying friends, there would have been plenty. What they need is not admonishing. Tell a frightened person to pull himself together and you have made him worse. Comfort them.

Help the weak. The verb (antechomai) means to hold on to, to cling to, to support: the word for taking someone’s arm. The weak may be weak in faith, in conscience, in body or in circumstance. What they need is not advice or exhortation, but someone bearing some of the weight.

The most practical sentence about pastoral care. Set the three together and you have the most practical sentence about pastoral care in the New Testament. Three different troubles require three different responses, and giving the wrong one does damage. The lazy man comforted stays lazy; the frightened man rebuked despairs; the weak man exhorted simply falls over. Wise care diagnoses before it treats.

Each one as the Lord treated them. Paul is not inventing a technique. He is describing how the Lord Jesus dealt with people. He warned the careless plainly, as in the parable of the servant who buried his master’s money and blamed his fear (Matthew 25:24–27). To terrified men in a boat at night he said, Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid (Matthew 14:27). And when Peter began to sink, Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him (Matthew 14:31), the very gesture that the word help describes. A church that warns, encourages and holds up the weak is doing to one another what its Lord has been doing to each of them.

Be patient with them all. Then the clause that makes it possible. Makrothymeō: long-tempered, slow to boil. It covers all three categories, because all three will try you: the idle will not start, the fainthearted will not be reassured, the weak will need holding up again next week. Patience is what keeps you doing the right thing for the eleventh time.

What it does not mean. It does not mean one approach fits all. Warning the fainthearted crushes them; comforting the idle confirms them.

How do I know which one a person needs? Listen before you speak, and ask questions. Is the problem that they will not, or that they cannot, or that they are afraid? The idle person usually knows what to do and is not doing it; the fainthearted person wants to but is crushed by fear; the weak person is willing but lacks strength. Many people are a mixture, and the same person can need different things in different seasons. Pray for wisdom (James 1:5), take time to know people, and be willing to change your approach when you see you have misjudged.

What if I am the fainthearted or the weak one? Then this verse is God’s instruction to your church to care for you, and there is no shame in receiving it. Tell someone honestly how you are. Let others hold your arm. You do not have to pretend to be strong in order to belong. The Lord does not break a bruised reed or quench a smouldering wick (Isaiah 42:3), and he has told his people to treat you the same way.

In a sentence. And we urge you, brothers and sisters, warn those who are idle and disruptive, encourage the disheartened, help the weak, be patient with everyone.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone you know. Do they need warning, encouragement or help? Give it, with patience. And if you are tempted to give everyone the same treatment, the one that comes most easily to you, ask God to make you wiser.

For worship. Before we were ever told to be patient with them all, he was patient with us: with the idle who would not follow, the fainthearted who ran, the weak who could not keep awake one hour. Paul himself was the proof. In him, the foremost of sinners, Christ Jesus displayed his perfect patience as an example to all who would believe (1 Timothy 1:16). He has not given up on one of his own, and every slow-tempered word we give a struggling brother is drawn from that bottomless supply. Blessed be the long-suffering Lord, who is not finished with any of us yet.
verseByVerse.note: “Idle” may mean those who had stopped working, perhaps expecting the Lord’s imminent return.

verseByVerse.quote: See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, but always seek to do good to one another and to everyone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, but always seek to do good to one another and to everyone.

See that no one repays anyone evil for evil. Not merely do not repay evil, but see to it that no one does: retaliation is made a community problem, not a private one (Romans 12:17; 1 Peter 3:9). And these were people under real hostility: driven from families, squeezed out of trades, watching their teacher run out of town. They had genuine grievances against identifiable neighbours. This is not an abstract ethic offered to the comfortable.

But always seek to do good to one another and to everyone. Then Paul goes past the prohibition: pursue the good of the people making your life hard. The verb (diōkō) means to chase after, the same word used for persecuting. They were being pursued with evil; they were to pursue with good, believers and everyone else, including persecutors.

The persecutor who was pursued. This is the teaching of Jesus, love your enemies, do good to those who hate you (Luke 6:27–28), and Paul had stood on the receiving end of it. He had once pursued the church, the same verb, and the risen Christ met him on the Damascus road asking, Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). The Lord did not repay. He chased his enemy down with mercy and made him an apostle. So when Paul tells a persecuted church to pursue good toward those pursuing them with evil, he is asking them to treat their enemies the way Christ treated him.

What makes it possible. This is among the hardest commands in Scripture, and two things in this letter make it possible. The Lord is an avenger (4:6), so the wronged Christian is not required to secure justice himself, because Someone else has undertaken to. And these people are not destined for wrath (5:9): they have received the exact treatment they are now being asked to extend. Refusing revenge is not pretending the wrong did not happen. It is handing it to a court that will actually deal with it, and treating your neighbour the way you were treated when you deserved otherwise.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ignoring justice. Governments punish evil (Romans 13:4). It means personal revenge is forbidden.

Does doing good to someone who hurt me mean I must trust them or stay near them? No. Doing good is not the same as giving access. You can refuse revenge, pray for someone and wish them well while keeping a safe distance, especially where there has been abuse or danger. Forgiveness releases the debt to God; trust is rebuilt only where there is real repentance and change, and sometimes not at all. Reporting a crime or seeking protection is not repaying evil for evil; it is seeking justice by the means God has given.

What does do good look like toward someone I resent? Small, concrete, real things. Speak of them fairly. Refuse to join in mockery. Pray for their blessing, and mean it as far as you can. Help them when they are in need. Answer a sharp word with a gentle one. You may not feel love at first, but deeds of good often lead the heart, and they always honour Christ.

In a sentence. Make sure that nobody pays back wrong for wrong, but always strive to do what is good for each other and for everyone else.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you want to pay back, even in small ways: the cold shoulder, the cutting remark, the story told to others? Ask God for grace to do them good instead, and choose one good thing to do for them this week.

For worship. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but entrusted himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). With nails through his hands he prayed for the men who drove them (Luke 23:34). Every evil the world could do was done to him, and he answered it with the one good that could save the world. Glory to the Lamb who overcame evil with good, and whose blood speaks a better word than vengeance (Hebrews 12:24).

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.

Three short commands. Three commands, seven words in Greek, among the best-known lines Paul ever wrote, and on first reading impossible.

Rejoice always. The shortest verse in the Greek New Testament by letters. Not: be cheerful about everything. Paul is not asking a grieving, persecuted church to pretend. Joy here is what it was in 1:6: joy given by the Holy Spirit in the middle of much affliction. It is possible always because its ground is outside the circumstances, joy in the Lord (Philippians 4:4), and that is the only reason it can be commanded at all.

Pray without ceasing. The word (adialeiptōs) does not mean uninterrupted. It was used of a persistent cough: something that keeps recurring, that never fully goes away. Paul is not requiring perpetual formal prayer, which would make ordinary work impossible. He is describing a life in which the line to God is never actually closed: regular times of prayer, and between them the running commentary of a heart that keeps turning to him through the day.

Give thanks in all circumstances. The preposition matters to a suffering reader: in all circumstances, not for all circumstances. Paul does not ask anyone to be grateful for evil, for a death, for a betrayal. He asks for thanksgiving to continue inside such things, because God’s goodness does not pause when circumstances turn, and he is at work in all of them (Romans 8:28). Anyone who has sat with a bereaved Christian who could still thank God for something has seen it done.

For this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you. Then the sentence that binds them. It is the second time the letter has told us plainly what God’s will is; the first was sanctification (4:3). People agonise over discovering God’s will as though it were hidden. Two things at least are published: he wants you holy, and he wants you rejoicing, praying and thankful. The three are held together for a reason: joy without prayer becomes shallow optimism; prayer without thanksgiving becomes a list of complaints; thanksgiving without joy becomes a duty.

On the night he was betrayed. And all of it is in Christ Jesus. Paul knew of a thanksgiving offered in the darkest circumstances there have ever been: on the night when he was betrayed the Lord Jesus took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it (1 Corinthians 11:23–24). He gave thanks with the cross a few hours away, over bread that meant his own body given. This will of God is not an ideal we strain toward alone. It is the life of the Son, who rejoiced, prayed and gave thanks perfectly, now lived out by his Spirit in those joined to him. Our thanks in hard places is an echo of his.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faking happiness or denying sorrow. Christians lament too. But beneath lament is joy and thanks.

How can I rejoice when I am grieving or depressed? Christian joy is not the same as a happy mood, and it can coexist with tears and even with dark seasons of the mind. The psalms of lament are full of sorrow, and most of them still turn toward God and end with trust. Joy at its root is the settled fact that Christ is yours and you are his, and you can hold on to that even when you cannot feel it. If you are depressed, seek help from your doctor as well as your church; that is not a lack of faith. And let others rejoice on your behalf for a while, and pray for you, until joy returns.

How do I pray without ceasing in a busy life? Build habits that keep the line open. Keep regular times of prayer, morning and evening if you can. Then attach short prayers to ordinary moments: waking, meals, the commute, the start of a meeting, a hard email, a piece of good news. Turn worries into requests the moment they arise, and turn pleasures into thanks. Over time, turning to God becomes a reflex, like the persistent cough Paul’s word describes.

In a sentence. Rejoice always, pray continually, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Practise all three today. At three set moments, morning, midday and evening, name one reason to rejoice in God, bring one request to him, and give thanks for one thing in your present circumstances, however hard they are. Then let the habit spread into the hours in between.

For worship. The God who commands our joy is himself the fountain of it, and he has given us everything in his Son. He is always listening, so prayer need never cease. He is always good, so thanks need never stop. And in Christ Jesus, the Man of Sorrows who for the joy set before him endured the cross, our joy has a foundation no grief can wash away. Blessed be the God of all joy, who has made his Son’s gladness ours.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good. Abstain from every form of evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good. Abstain from every form of evil.

Do not quench the Spirit. Five short commands about the Spirit’s work in the assembly move in order: two prohibitions, the corrective, then its two outcomes. The verb (sbennymi) is used of putting out a fire, and the metaphor is deliberate: the Spirit is spoken of as flame (Acts 2:3). You do not extinguish a fire by attacking it; you do it by smothering it, or by simply not feeding it. He can be stifled by sin, by neglect, or by suppressing his work in the church. The next line suggests one way.

Do not despise prophecies. Evidently some in Thessalonica were dismissive of prophetic speech in the meeting. One can see why: the second letter has to deal with a claimed message saying the day of the Lord had already come (2 Thessalonians 2:2). When people have been misled by something claiming the Spirit’s authority, the instinct is to shut the whole thing down.

But test everything. Paul refuses that instinct, and his answer is the balance the church has needed ever since. Not credulity, which accepts whatever is confidently asserted. Not cynicism, which rejects everything to be safe. Testing: dokimazō, the assayer’s word from 2:4, weighing metal to see whether it is genuine (1 John 4:1). In the apostolic church the remedy for false prophecy was not contempt for prophecy but discernment; and now that the apostolic word stands complete in Scripture, every claim to speak for God is tested against it.

What the Spirit always says. Testing is not guesswork, because the Spirit has one consistent subject. He will glorify me, Jesus said, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you (John 16:14). So the New Testament’s tests all turn on Christ: no one speaking by the Spirit says Jesus is accursed, and no one can say Jesus is Lord except by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3); every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God (1 John 4:2). A word that makes much of the speaker or the experience, and little of the crucified and risen Lord, has already failed.

Hold fast what is good. Testing has two results, one in each direction. Hold fast what is good: grip it, keep what passes the test. Discernment that only ever rejects has failed at half its job. And abstain from every form of evil: whatever the testing shows to be bad, drop it entirely, whatever authority was claimed for it.

Every form, or all appearance? The KJV reads abstain from all appearance of evil, and it has often been taken to mean avoiding anything that might look wrong to others. The ESV’s every form of evil is the better rendering: Paul means to shun evil in every shape it takes, not to live by other people’s impressions. Avoiding needless offence is wise, but that is not the point of this verse.

Does this mean prophecy continues today? At Thessalonica, before the New Testament was written, prophets spoke words from the Spirit in the gathered church, and Paul tells the church to weigh them, not despise them. Continuationist Christians believe such prophecy continues. The more likely reading is that prophecy as new revelation belonged with the apostles to the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20), and ceased when the Scriptures were complete. The principle stands: test everything; hold fast what is good. Every claim to speak for God must be tested by his written word.

Where Christians differ: prophecy today. Continuationists see here a command for churches to welcome prophecy today; some cessationists dismiss the passage. Verdict: In the apostolic churches, before the New Testament was complete, prophecy was an active gift, and Paul commanded the church neither to despise nor accept it uncritically. With the completion of Scripture, revelatory prophecy has ceased (Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 1:1–2). But the principles remain: do not quench the Spirit, who speaks through the word; test every teaching and claim by Scripture; hold to what is good. These apply to preaching, teaching and every claim of spiritual guidance today. This view is held with charity toward continuationist brothers and sisters.

Open, and awake. The five refuse both of the easy positions. A church can be so afraid of disorder that it quenches the Spirit, or so afraid of quenching the Spirit that it swallows anything. Paul asks for the harder combination: open, and awake.

What it does not mean. It does not mean being suspicious of everything. It means discernment.

How might a cessationist church quench the Spirit? By treating the Bible as a museum piece rather than the living voice of God; by preaching without prayer or dependence on the Spirit; by resisting conviction of sin; by stifling the gifts he does give, such as teaching, encouragement, mercy and service; or by a coldness that never expects God to change anyone. The Spirit speaks through the word, so the surest way to quench him is to stop listening to Scripture expectantly. Cessationism rightly guards the closed canon; it must never become an excuse for spiritual deadness.

What if someone tells me God gave them a word for me? Listen respectfully, then test it by Scripture. If it contradicts the Bible, reject it, however sincere the speaker. If it is simply a biblical truth applied, such as a reminder of God’s promises or a warning against a sin Scripture names, you may receive it as good counsel, but its authority comes from Scripture, not from the claim. Do not make major decisions on the basis of such words alone. Ask wise, mature believers and your pastors. God’s will for you is found in his written word and in wise, prayerful obedience to it.

In a sentence. Do not quench the Spirit. Do not treat prophecies with contempt but test them all; hold on to what is good, reject every kind of evil.

On a Tuesday. Test what you hear today, from preachers, books, podcasts and social media, by Scripture. Keep what is good, and drop what is not, whoever said it. And ask the Spirit to keep the fire burning in you by his word.

For worship. The Spirit of God is a fire, and he has kindled flame in cold hearts. He gave the prophets their words and the apostles their gospel, and he has given the church a finished Scripture by which every voice can be weighed. He is the Spirit of truth, who never contradicts the word he breathed. Blessed be the Holy Spirit, who leads us into all the truth and keeps us faithful to Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: 5:23–28 – Kept Blameless, and the Last Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul prays that the God of peace will make them holy through and through and keep them whole and blameless until the coming of the Lord Jesus; the God who calls them is faithful and will do it. He asks for their prayers, sends greetings with a holy kiss, insists that the letter be read to all the believers, and ends with the grace of the Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.theology:
Whole Persons, and Who Does the Keeping

‘Spirit and soul and body’ (v.23) is a way of saying the whole of you, and they are to be kept — passive — by the God who calls them and is faithful (v.24).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The oath of verse 27 ensured the letter reached every believer, the illiterate and the fainthearted included.

Now: The holy kiss for all the brothers (v.26) is a quiet demolition of rank: you cannot greet someone as family every week and go on regarding him as beneath you.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, and may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, and may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it.

Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely. The letter turns to prayer. The God of peace: the God who makes peace with sinners through the blood of his Son. Himself: not an angel, not a programme. Paul has told them to be holy, to work, to love, to stay awake, to test everything. Now he prays, because he knows that nobody produces this by effort. Sanctification is finally God’s work. And it is complete: holoteleis, a compound of whole and end, through and through, right to the finish.

And may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless. Nothing is left outside: the whole person. And be kept (tēreō, guarded, preserved) is passive. They are not keeping themselves. Someone is keeping them, and the difference between those two sentences is the difference between exhaustion and rest. The goal is the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ: every chapter of this letter has ended with his coming, and this one does too.

Blameless before whom? How can anyone who knows his own heart be without blame when the Lord Jesus comes? Paul answers elsewhere: Christ has reconciled us in his body of flesh by his death, in order to present us holy and blameless and above reproach before him (Colossians 1:22). The one before whom we must stand is the one who made us fit to stand. His death gives the blamelessness that counts before God now, and his Spirit works it out in spirit, soul and body, until the day we see him and are made like him (1 John 3:2).

Three parts or two? The threefold phrase raises an old question: is a person made of three parts or two? Some have read it as trichotomy: spirit as the God-ward faculty, soul as the conscious self, body as the physical frame, three compartments. The historic Reformed reading, from Calvin on, is dichotomy: spirit and soul name the one immaterial dimension of human nature from two angles, not two separate parts. Scripture sets the words side by side in parallel (Luke 1:46–47), and the pattern is familiar from Deuteronomy 6:5, love the LORD with all your heart and soul and might, which nobody takes as an anatomy. It is a way of saying the whole of you.

Where Christians differ: spirit, soul and body. Some (trichotomists) take this to mean humans have three distinct parts: spirit, soul and body. Others (dichotomists) hold two: body and soul (or spirit). Verdict: Scripture usually describes humans as body and soul, or body and spirit, using soul and spirit interchangeably (Matthew 10:28; 1 Corinthians 7:34; Ecclesiastes 12:7). Paul here stresses the whole person, every aspect, not giving a technical anatomy. The majority Reformed view is that humans are a unity of body and soul (Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 10; Larger Catechism Q. 17).

Where Christians differ: entire sanctification. Some in the Wesleyan tradition take this verse to teach that believers can be sanctified entirely in this life, free from sin. Verdict: Paul prays for complete sanctification, and God will accomplish it, at the coming of Christ. In this life, believers grow in holiness but remain sinners (1 John 1:8). Sanctification is complete at glorification (Philippians 3:12; Westminster 13.2).

He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it. Then the prayer becomes a promise. The calling is present tense, as in 2:12: he goes on calling. And the guarantee is not their staying power but his character. Paul has just asked God for something enormous, and then tells them it is as good as done, because the one being asked does not begin what he will not finish (Philippians 1:6; 1 Corinthians 1:8–9).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we are passive. But it rests our hope on God’s faithfulness, not our strength.

If God will do it, why should I make any effort? Because God sanctifies us through our effort, not instead of it. Paul can say in one breath, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work (Philippians 2:12–13). His promise is not a reason to stop fighting sin but the reason the fight is not hopeless. You strive because he is at work, and you rest because the outcome depends on him. Effort without the promise leads to despair; the promise without effort is a misreading of it.

Does my body matter to God as much as my soul? Yes. Paul prays for body as well as spirit and soul to be kept blameless. God made the body, the Son took a body, the Spirit dwells in the body, and the body will be raised. So what you do with your body, sexual purity, honest work, care for health, rest, and the use of your eyes, hands and tongue, is part of your holiness. Christianity is not a religion that despises the physical. It sanctifies it.

In a sentence. May God himself, the God of peace, sanctify you through and through. May your whole spirit, soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. The one who calls you is faithful, and he will do it.

On a Tuesday. When you feel discouraged at how slowly you are changing, read verse 24 aloud: he who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it. Then take the next small step of obedience in front of you, and leave the finishing to him.

For worship. The God of peace does not leave his work half done. He kept every promise from Abraham to Bethlehem, and when his Son lay dead he brought him again from the dead, the great shepherd of the sheep, by the blood of the eternal covenant (Hebrews 13:20). That same faithfulness stands behind this prayer. On the day of Christ every believer will stand whole and blameless, spirit, soul and body, kept by the hand that raised Jesus. Glory to the God of peace, whose calling is as sure as an empty tomb.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, pray for us. Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. I put you under oath before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers, pray for us. Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. I put you under oath before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers.

Brothers, pray for us. Three requests, each more revealing than it looks. The apostle who has prayed for them constantly (1:2), night and day (3:10), asks them to pray for him. He has just prayed for their sanctification, and asks for their prayers in return: the traffic does not run one way. Mutual intercession is the life of the church.

Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. The kiss on the cheek was an ordinary greeting in that world, between family and close friends, and it became the family greeting of the early church (Romans 16:16). What is not ordinary is the range Paul gives it: all the brothers, including the idle and the fainthearted. In a room containing slaves and masters, Jews and Greeks, men and women, the wealthy householder and the day labourer, that instruction dismantles something. You cannot greet a man as family every week and go on regarding him as beneath you. The adjective holy distinguishes it from the ordinary social kiss: this one is set apart, and it means what it says.

Must Christians greet one another with a kiss today? The command is for a warm, sincere greeting between brothers and sisters, in the form one’s culture uses. Where a kiss carries that meaning, it may still be used; elsewhere a handshake or an embrace obeys the command. What matters is that no one in the church is left ungreeted, and that the greeting is pure and genuine.

I put you under oath before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers. Then the third, and the tone shifts sharply. The verb is strong: to adjure, to place someone under solemn obligation. Why so forceful? Almost certainly because of the word all. Letters were read aloud to the gathered church; most believers met Scripture with their ears, and many could not read. Paul wants nobody left out: not the illiterate, not the slaves who might not be at every meeting, not the fainthearted and the weak he has just named. He has written things in this letter that grieving and frightened people need, and he will not have it circulate among a few.

Before the Lord. The oath is sworn by the Lord, which in this letter almost always means Jesus. It is Christ’s word Paul is sending. They had received his preaching not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God (2:13), and Jesus had said of his messengers that whoever hears them hears him (Luke 10:16). So the letter is to be read to the whole assembly, as the Scriptures were read in the synagogue (Colossians 4:16), which is not how anyone treats private correspondence. To read it to every brother and sister is to let the Lord himself speak to the whole of his flock. To keep it from any of them would be to stand between the Shepherd and his sheep.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Scripture is only for leaders. It is for all God’s people.

How should I pray for my pastor and for missionaries? Pray as Paul asked elsewhere: that the word of the Lord may speed ahead and be honoured, that they may be delivered from wicked people (2 Thessalonians 3:1–2), that doors would open for the gospel and they would speak it clearly (Colossians 4:3–4), and that they would be bold (Ephesians 6:19–20). Pray for their holiness, their marriages and children, their health and their joy. Ask them what they need prayer for, and then tell them you prayed.

In a sentence. Brothers and sisters, pray for us. Greet all God’s people with a holy kiss. Paul charges you before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers and sisters.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your pastor and for one missionary by name today. Greet someone at church this Sunday you usually pass by. And make sure Scripture is read aloud in your home, so that no one under your roof is left out.

For worship. The Lord has given his word to all his people, not to a few. He puts it into the ears of slaves and children and the unlettered, and it makes them wise for salvation. He has made us one family, greeting one another as brothers and sisters, and joined us in prayer for one another. Blessed be the God whose word is for all, and whose family has room for everyone who comes to his Son.
verseByVerse.note: The holy kiss was the family greeting of the early church.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. The letter opened with grace (1:1) and closes with it, and the two form a frame around everything between. That is not a formality; it is a statement about what the whole thing is made of. Inside the frame stand a young church under persecution, a congregation burying its dead, a man defending himself against slander, and a list of commands most of us find hard. All of it sits inside grace.

Grace arriving, grace staying. Notice the small change from the greeting. There Paul wrote grace to you: grace arriving. Here it is grace be with you: grace staying, accompanying them into whatever came next. He could not come himself; Satan had blocked the road and Timothy had gone in his place. What he can send is this.

What came next. What came next was not easy. They would go on being a small, pressured minority in a proud Roman city. Paul would write a second letter, probably within months, because the confusion about the Lord’s coming had got worse. The last word he gives them is the thing that would still be true through all of it. Like every one of Paul’s letters, this one ends not with an exhortation or a warning but with grace, the one provision that does not run out.

Grace with a name. Paul uses the same phrase when he wants to show what grace looks like: you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). Grace has a name and a history: the Son leaving glory, taking flesh and dying for us (5:10). When the letter ends with grace, it ends with him, and the blessing is that he goes with them into whatever comes.

What it does not mean. It does not mean grace is earned by the obedience commanded in the letter. Grace makes that obedience possible.

What is grace, exactly? Grace is God’s free, undeserved favour toward sinners in Christ, and his power at work in them. It is favour: God treats us not as our sins deserve but as his Son deserves. And it is power: the same grace that forgives also changes, strengthens and keeps (2 Corinthians 12:9; Titus 2:11–12). It is the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ because he is its source and its channel: he bought it at the cross and gives it from the throne. Every command in this letter is obeyed by it, and every promise is kept by it.

In a sentence. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

On a Tuesday. Whatever this week holds, begin and end it here: the grace of the Lord Jesus is with you. When you fail, it forgives. When you are weak, it strengthens. When you are afraid, it keeps. Live today inside the frame.

For worship. The grace the Lord gave a frightened church in a proud city has not grown thin with use. It began before the world was made, was poured out at the cross, carried the Thessalonians through persecution and grief, and holds his people now; and it will bring them home on the day of his coming. From the first word of the letter to the last, and from the first word of our story to the last, it is all grace, and the glory is all his.
